text:
I’m building my first PC. I’ve been assembling parts for the last week or so and I’ll be ready to assemble everything tomorrow, provided my final amazon shipment arrives on time. 

I could have purchased a 2080ti but I eventually decided to go with EVGA’s 2070 Super FTW3 Ultra+ (ridiculous name, I know). My thinking went as follows: I’m getting into the game fairly late in the product cycle. Nvidia will most likely be rolling out a new batch of RTX cards pretty soon so do I really want to drop $1,300 on my first graphics card a few months before the next generation is announced? Of course the 2080ti is a great performer but the sense I’ve gotten from most people is that while it is really freaking good, it just isn’t really worth the money right now. Also, it looks like A LOT of them have had to be RMA’d. Reviews on Asus’ ROG Strix version are particularly worrying but I saw what seemed like a ton of issues from cards made by various manufacturers. 

The fact that I’m getting in late in the production cycle is also part of why I went for the Ryzen 3700X, the Aorus Ultra x570 board and a Gen4 NVMe SSD. I didn’t want to buy a B450 this late it’s lifetime and I wanted to have access to cool next-gen features for the next couple of years without having to replace any major hardware. AM4 is supposedly going to be supported by AMD for another generation of Ryzen processors which made spending a little more on the motherboard make sense to me. 

Basically, I went for the 2070 Super because I want a damn good 1440p setup but didn’t want to buy a $1,300 video card when the next gen version might be heavily improved and possibly even cheaper. If I spent that kind of money on a 2080ti and then a few months later, the 2180ti was announced for $900, I’d probably be a little pissed off. Not saying I think the price will come down that much but it could come down after the constant complaints from customers and reviewers. I think that the 2070 Super will give me the performance I’m looking for and allow me to save that extra $700+ for when a card that I REALLY want comes out. Another thing, ray tracing is really cool but it’s not really a selling point right now because it’s just too new and too poorly optimized so there isn’t really a need for me to have the absolute last word in performance in order to run it. Once it’s more widely implemented and more optimized, I’ll definitely be looking at picking up a XX80ti.

text:
So you are willing to pay extra for a feature that barely works on the 2080Ti and you will not be able to use  on this card with only 8GB of RAM.  Ray Tracing is a gimmick, albeit a good one, to justify this price hike.  Just my opinion but fake lighting is really good, Ray Tracing is great. I am happy paying less for really good with faster frames.  No need for a 4K monitor with over 60hz refresh if turning on Ray Tracing gives you below 60hz.  You might as well go backwards and get a 1080P monitor to keep the refresh up but now you have a lower overall resolution so the lighting will look a little better.  WHAT.


I bought a Radeon VII for $1073 after taxes with 3 "free" games that I planned on getting eventually.  Those 3 games list for a total of $270 after taxes here in Canada so technically the card cost me $803.  
I have a liquid cooled system so I bought an EK water block costing around $270 after taxes and shipping bringing the cost of the card back up to around $1100.  


I think I know why some people are still getting high temps with a water block installed. The risers to install the back plate loosen when removing it.  I could see that the card was warped because of this.  I removed the back plate, put some red Loctite on the risers and reinstalled with no warping.  The Loctite is not necessary, I had some so I used it.  Just on the risers screwing into the board, not the screws holding the backplate on the board.  Do not do that.  The block will need cleaning eventually but the risers stay on for that.


My temps average between 36 and 46 degrees C depending on the game with an OC of 1901 core @ 1152 mv, power limit of 14%, memory clocked @ 1144, memory timing of 2 on a 24/7 OC'd I7 5930K running at 4.18GHZ at an avg of 38 C, no voltage increase.  My CPU and GPU will easily go faster but I currently do not need faster.  


My LG monitor runs at 3440x1440 @ 75hz.  I also have an Oculus Rift and if you built a min spec PC for VR it will suck.  I previously owned 2) Fury X's hoping Liquid VR was going to be a real thing.  I believe only Serious Sam supported that.  I chose wrong.  This card was what VR needed along with the 1080Ti and up.  If you have to turn all of your features off to play in VR it will suck.  Not really a news flash as to why VR is not as popular as it should be.  Too many people have had a terrible experience in VR to want to get it.  Lucky was right to hold back the release ( I wanted it sooner like everyone else ) and if HTC would have waited a year longer the initial release would have been met with better, more VR friendly PC hardware.



I upgrade my system every 4 years, roughly.  With liquid cooling and 16GB of HBM2 I feel like I can stretch my cards purpose to at least four years. 


I know people are going to say for that price I could have bought the RTX 2080 Ti.  At the time of purchase the RTX 2080Ti in Canada was going for between $1700 and $2500 on Amazon.ca.  Hard GFY.  I liquid cool my PC for a couple reasons and one is to keep my computer room cool because I am always hot.  Especially in VR.  I would need to buy a WB for that card as well.  The 2080Ti is the most powerful card available even without Ray Tracing but not at that price point.  Not even close.


I am not a fanboy "sheep" of any corporation, wake up.  I have owned many GPU's from other companies over the years including Trident, Matrox, 3DFX, and Nvidia along with numerous ATI cards.  Unfortunately my love for 3DFX did not carry over to the company that acquired it.  My first PC was a Tandy 1000 SX.  I also loved my Gravis Ultrasound MAX with 512KB of memory.  I am old but I greatly appreciate where we are technically, even though many companies, patents, are holding us back.  Most nostalgic moments have a time stamp locked in history.  Meaning I have no desire to go back to any old tech, no matter how much I loved it at the time.


I miss having more competition in the GPU arena.


Sorry, not sorry for rambling.

text:
@cmdrflint9115  It would be nearly impossible for PS5 to be less powerful than the 2070, and highly unlikely that it would be under 2080 performance.
Don't forget PC benchmarks are rarely optimized for AMD hardware, vs PS5 where first party games are inherently optimized for AMD.
Vega 64 is already equal to the 2070 in some cases and we know 5700XT is ~15% faster than Vega 64, and we know PS5 is not using 5700XT, it's still got a year of development before release and will be better.
PS5 is totally custom hardware and Sony can put any number of CUs they want in PS5.
If they want to beat 2080Ti that is not outside the realm of possibility.
author: @budthecyborg4575

text:
@budthecyborg4575  in all likelihood the ps5 will be using a cut down 5700xt, no way are they going to squeeze a full desktop gpu onto an APU and certainly not when the desktop part costs $400+, not to mention the thernal and power budget they have to stick to. 

While I am a bit sceptical of the claim of 20'000 points in firestrike that's been leaked around various places for the ps5, it would certainly fit with the ps5 being in the range of a 2070.

There simply is no way they would release ps5 at anything close to 2080ti performance, AMD dont have a gpu anywhere close to that right now, their fastest card is the $700 radeon 7, which is a 2080 equivalent.

No doubt console optimisation would see it punching above its weight, afterall, in some games the xbox 1x performs almost on par with a gtx1070, despite having a lower tier gpu, optimisation for specific hardware goes a long way.

This gen of consoles isnt about the GPU upgrade, why do you think they're not shouting about tflops this time round, but focussing on the CPU upgrade instead. 

I guess we will see in about a years time, feel free to come back and tell me I was wrong :)
author: @cmdrflint9115

text:
@cmdrflint9115  "There simply is no way they would release ps5 at anything close to 2080ti performance, AMD dont have a gpu anywhere close to that right now"
https://www.techspot.com/review/1865-geforce-rtx-super/

In Battlefield V at 1440p Vega 64+15% is within 22% of the 2080Ti.
(Also see Forza Horison 4, Far Cry New Dawn, and World War Z.)

The 5700XT has a 251mm die size, PS4 launched with a 348mm die size.

A 48CU version of the 5700XT would not be difficult to fit in PS5, but remember PS5 GPU architecture will be slightly better than the 5700XT and Sony's first party games (what everyone buys the console for) will be even more optimized for the hardware than BFV.


Given how ambitious the whole console is this time it would take a bit of Sony subsidizing the price to sell PS5 at the $499 price point with a GPU equal to 2080Ti, but it certainly could be done (and wouldn't even be out of the ordinary from a historical perspective).
Hitting base 5700XT specs at $399 would be the other option.

text:
AMD's NAVI 2019 looks to be a bad choice so far, but the PRICING also matters. The main reasons to consider NAVI would be:
a) if you think 8GB matters more than 6GB for a NAVI card that competes with RTX2060 card (so the NAVI card might have 8GB but the RTX2060 has the RT/Tensor cores. Both the extra VRAM and the RT/Tensor cores will get increasingly utilized as time goes by so it's a tough choice. I really don't think 6GB is quite enough but I also think RT/Tensor will start showing its value in 2021 after the consoles launch which are rumored to do ray-tracing reasonably often so we can expect hardware-based ray tracing for cross-platform PC games, or


b) You have a FREESYNC monitor that doesn't support GSync (there are GSync compatible Freesync monitors which means NVidia added driver support for some Freesync monitors that will work fine with GSync cards. Many don't, especially if they don't support LFC.)


c) If the NAVI FPS per Dollar value is higher.


*Personally, for any NVidia RTX2000 series with at least 8GB of VRAM I'd buy it over AMD NAVI even if the Dollar per FPS is slightly higher because of the added RT/Tensor value. At the same price I'd say if it gets 90% of the performance on average of NAVI I'd get an RTX2000 card (Super or not, though preferably Super due to the slight improvements).

text:
As a recent MSI Ventus RTX 2070 buyer, it's slightly annoying that the Super outperforms my card by 20 or more percent. That said, I could have spent 200 euro more on the same non-super 2070 platform for a better binned chip and cooling solution but originally I was looking at the lower end 1660 and 2060 and decided that an extra 150 euros for an entry level 2070 was the better choice. I could care less about the super 2070's sli option as my 2070 is has the power of four GTX 960's which is what I upgraded from. I did pause for thought when I watched the stuff about AMD's RX lineup especially the 5700XT but waiting a couple of months to buy a 3rd Party non-blower card that would, perhaps, slightly outperform the 2070 in rasterization but not support things like DLSS and RTX while drawing more wattage seemed like bad idea to me. 



My previous pc was an i5 4460 with a GTX 960 (2Gb with a blower) and 16gb of slightly mismatched Kingston 1600 ddr3 ram and I now have a Ryzen 5 2600 with an RTX 2070 and 16gb of Corsair LPX vengeance 3200 ddr4 ram. My previous system was pre-built and before that I had two "gaming" laptops (including the infamous Dell XPS 13 with the self-warping motherboard) so getting back up to speed about what the best hardware to get for my budget was made faaaar easier thanks to Gamers Nexus. So thanks guys for all the hard work delivering what some would consider tediously boring information, in an entertaining way. I look forward to many more months of watching my hardware slowly slipping down the graphs, triggering my next, well-informed, upgrade.

text:
0:20 - As I understand the pricing of the 2060 Super, it's faster but more expensive by a margin than is larger than the performance increase, so hardly listening to the community; more like just another attempt to upsell. Fact is, the entire stack is still far too expensive. It's as if the memory of what 60/70 cards used to be has just gone. The 2070 Super does see a price cut with a speed bump, but the pricing is still rotten (the 2070 is what the 2060 should have been, we can tell that from the die name and the lack of SLI). No pricing available in the UK yet, but pricing for existing models is still whacko. So congrats to those who buy a 2070 Super (sarcasm), that's what should have been a 2060 Ti.

25:48 - I hardly think NVIDIA "ends up looking good" for reducing prices to a point that's still massively higher than it should have been in the first place based on the performance offered. These products are still grossly overpriced, just as Navi looks like it will be aswell. The sensible recommendation to skip ALL of these cards. Don't buy them. I wish tech media would genuinely side with the consumer; atm "not an apple fan" is the only one keeping it real. If these changes were happening in isolation then perhaps they would be praiseworthy, but in a broader and historical context the new GPU market will stink just as much in a week's time as it does now.

text:
Thank you so much for being one of if not the first to start paying more attention to the importance of graphics APIs rather than just legacy DX11 performance, especially knowing the as of January 14, 2020, Microsoft will be terminating support for Windows 7 (extended support ending in 2023), the only thing IMHO really keeping DX11 relevant. Add to this Canonical, the guys behind the most popular Linux distribution, joining Microsoft in assertively reminding people including Valve that the writing is on the wall for 32-bit software including games and container type solutions will be required going forward. Not sure how it will play out but game devs will have to start writing their code for DX12 and/or Vulkan rather than what seems to be the current practice of writing for DX11 and then making lazy ports to DX12 and Vulkan. This is probably why DX12 suffers in performance relative to DX11. Vulkan being opensource has a wider community developing for it so it doesn't suffer as much. 

All that said, speaking as a Linux user and owner of both the AMD Radeon VII and Nvidia RTX 2080ti both bought at launch, I can safely say buyers remorse does not figure in anyway shape or form. It boils down to use case. It was expected that Nvidia would release something this year especially as AMD had already said they would be releasing graphics products every year going forward. Until the RTX 2080ti Super comes out with at least 16GB VRAM and cuda and RTX core counts just shy of the Titan RTX, I am fine with my 2080ti. An incremental change like 2070 to 2070 Super is great, but it is not 1070 vs 980ti change. So at this late stage it is nothing more that would be expected from a 1070ti vs 1070.

As for the Radeon VII, it was always an opportunistic play by AMD and sold as a Workstation GPU that did near high-end gaming. Add to this for users of Linux where Vulkan and OpenCL are the native APIs, both of which Nvidia hardware have tended to be terrible at, the Radeon VII still remains a strong option if you takie into account the texture issues all Nvidia GPUs have; even the RTX 2080ti. Granted Linux is a tiny use case even if many Windows users are starting to switch to or experiment with Linux.

IMHO there's little that is meaningful about any of the GPUs released these past 12 or so months. Next year is the time people should really start thinking of buying new GPUs till then it is used

text:

SLI sucks. I investigated the current state of it and it's still a mess. A game might get more STUTTER than you would without SLI. I'm not even sure if you can force it on a per-game basis easily. I'd at least want SLI to be OFF by default then force it on manually only for games I want. Anyway, pretty much every tech expert I respect says to avoid SLI or Crossfire... where I'd recommend spending money at some point if you have not is a GSYNC monitor (or GSync compatible Freesync monitor). Note that with 4K monitors you need to limit to 98Hz with 4:4:4 10-bit, so I'd wait and get a 4K monitor that supports DSC (Display Stream Compression) which needs the monitor and graphics card BOTH to support. I believe the RTX2000 series supports DSC (I think GTX1000 does too, but I'm confused on whether DSC being in the DP1.4 spec means it MUST be supported or whether it's optional).

Also its pretty easy to get a MB that has a switch to enable/disable either of the cards or it can be done on the software side. It's a good thing to do for some graphics cards, and CPUs as well, depending on what you're trying to do with them. For Vega, it's good to undervolt because it allows the card to run cooler and, because of that, run higher clocks. It's not the only consideration, but that's the gist of it.

author: @Junior305able

text: @AmusiaPrussia I'm 100% sure they are testing reference cards for AMD's vega cards. Vega 56 is volt limited on the HBM2 and will cap out around 900-950mhz on HBM2. Flashing a Vega 64 bios over the 56 on reference cards increases the voltage limit of HBM2 to 1.356v allowing higher HBM overclocks up to 1100-1150 with a better cooling solution, stock configuration can push 1000-1100 depending on temps and quality. Its crazy to think that a stock Vega 56, without tampering with it too much, leaves almost 20% performance on the table. My 2nd hand Vega 56 bios is flashed and undervolted/overclocked on core and memory and with a Morpheus 2, it probably performs on par if not better than a stock 2070 all for just under $400 a year and a half ago.
